reason: Start with developing red cells and their haemoglobin, which should lead toward the oxygen-binding goal.
expectation: I expect the cells to make haemoglobin from the supplied materials, though further maturation may be needed.

alternatives.reason: Making plasma also supports the blood-assembly goal, but I want to follow the oxygen-carrying cells first.

effect: The cells have matured and assembled haemoglobin, so I can now test oxygen binding.
reaction: The developing-cell cutaway makes the transition to nucleus-free red cells clear.
reason: Combine the red cells with oxygen to pursue the reversible-binding goal.
expectation: I expect oxygen to bind to haemoglobin in the red cells; a separate step may be needed to show release.

alternatives.reason: Plasma is needed for blood assembly, but I want to follow the oxygen route first.

effect: The double arrow and explanation show both oxygen binding and release, completing that goal; blood assembly remains.
reaction: The link between low dissolved oxygen in working tissues and oxygen release is useful.
reason: Make plasma as the only offered combination toward assembling blood.
expectation: I expect the water and solutes to form plasma, ready to combine with blood cells.

effect: Plasma is ready to combine with the cellular components of blood.
reaction: The straw-yellow drop makes the fluid component easy to distinguish.
reason: Add the oxygen-bearing red cells to plasma, continuing the oxygen-carrying route while assembling blood.
expectation: I expect a plasma-and-red-cell mixture that still needs white cells and platelets.

alternatives.reason: Adding white cells and platelets first also contributes to assembly, but I chose to add the red cells first.

effect: The partial sample contains red cells in plasma but still lacks white cells and platelets.
reaction: The explicit partial-sample description makes the remaining step clear.
reason: Add the missing cellular components; this is the only offered combination.
expectation: I expect a blood sample containing plasma, oxygen-bearing red cells, white cells and platelets.

effect: The completed sample brings plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets together, finishing the blood-assembly goal.
reaction: The final picture clearly distinguishes the components, though it says little about what white cells and platelets do.

mostWorthwhile.text: Binding oxygen to red cells was most worthwhile: the planned double arrow and explanation connect reversible haemoglobin binding to oxygen release in working tissues.

leastWorthwhile.text: Making plasma and then adding red cells felt relatively procedural; the partial sample clearly showed what remained, but added little explanation beyond the component list.

surprise.text: The oxygen-binding result showed release as well as binding in one step, so no separate release action was needed.

arbitrary.text: Adding red cells before white cells and platelets was an arbitrary ordering choice; either component group was offered for plasma, and I had no biological reason to prefer that order.

continue.text: I would continue for another chapter to see how circulation brings oxygen carriers close to cells; this chapter establishes that connection but does not show the route.
